blocks.prompt: The Whale That Is Really a Dolphin
blocks.text: An orca looks like a whale. But an orca is really a dolphin. It is the biggest dolphin in the sea. An orca is black on top and white underneath. There is a white patch behind each eye. On its back is a tall fin. Orcas live in a family called a pod. The oldest mom leads the pod. She knows where the food is. She remembers it from long ago. Baby orcas stay with their mom. Some stay with her their whole life. Orcas talk to each other. They squeak and click and whistle. Each pod has its own way of talking. An orca can hear its family from far away.

blocks.prompt: The Biggest Dolphin in the World
blocks.text: The orca is not a whale at all. It is a dolphin, the largest one on Earth. A big male can grow as long as a school bus and weigh more than a truck. The tall fin on his back can stand six feet high. Orcas live everywhere. They swim in warm water near the equator and under the ice at both poles. No other mammal except people lives in so many places. An orca family is called a pod, and it is built around one old female. She is the grandmother, and she may be eighty years old. She has stopped having calves of her own, but she has not stopped working. When food is scarce, she leads the pod to the places where she found salmon decades ago. Her memory feeds everybody. Each pod also has its own set of calls. Scientists call it a dialect, like an accent. Orcas from one pod can hear a stranger's calls and know at once that they are not family.

blocks.prompt: Skills Nobody Is Born With
blocks.text: Off the coast of Norway, orcas circle a school of herring, tighter and tighter, until the fish are packed into a silver ball. Then one orca swings its tail through the ball like a bat. The blow stuns dozens of herring at once, and the pod eats them as they drift. Off the coast of Argentina, orcas do something no sensible sea animal should do. They ride a wave straight up onto a gravel beach, grab a sea lion pup, and wriggle backward into the water. A mistake means being stranded and dying in the sun. In Antarctica, a seal rests on a floating sheet of ice. Several orcas line up shoulder to shoulder, swim hard at the ice together, and dive at the last moment. Their wake becomes a wave that washes the seal off. None of these are instincts. Not one orca is born knowing them. Each is a skill invented by somebody's grandmother and taught to the young over years of practice. Scientists call this culture, and until recently they thought only humans had it. Culture also decides what an orca will eat. In the same stretch of water, one group hunts only salmon and another hunts only seals. They speak different dialects. They avoid each other. They have not mixed for thousands of years, though nothing stops them but habit.

blocks.prompt: The Grandmother's Map
blocks.text: There are only a handful of animals on Earth in which females stop reproducing long before they die. Humans are one. Orcas are another. A female orca has her last calf somewhere around the age of forty, then lives on for another thirty, forty, sometimes fifty years. Evolution is not usually sentimental about individuals who cannot produce offspring. So why keep her? The answer is that she is the pod's library. Off the coast of Washington and British Columbia, one population of orcas eats almost nothing but Chinook salmon. Salmon runs move. They fail in some years and flood in others. Researchers who have tracked these families for decades noticed that when salmon are scarce, it is the oldest female who swims out front, choosing the route. In good years her leadership matters less. In hungry years it matters enormously. The numbers back it up. When a grandmother dies, her grandcalves are far more likely to die within the next two years, and the effect is strongest for her grandsons. She is not simply a comfort to have around. She is a survival advantage that can be measured in bodies. This is why the story of the Southern Residents is so hard to read. That population is down to roughly seventy animals. Their salmon have been dammed and fished away. Their water is loud with boat engines, and orcas hunt with sound, so noise is very nearly the same thing as darkness to them. Their fat carries industrial chemicals poured into the sea decades ago, and a mother passes much of her share to her first calf in her milk. Every grandmother that dies takes a map with her, and that map cannot be rebuilt from a book.

6.title: The Whale That Is Really a Dolphin
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Whale That Is Really a Dolphin

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Orcinus orca, largest of the dolphins
The name came from Spanish asesina de ballenas, killer of whales
Resident orcas eat fish; Bigg's orcas eat marine mammals
The two have not interbred in hundreds of thousands of years
Hunting traditions are local: Norway, Patagonia, Antarctica, New Zealand
Southern Residents: about seventy animals left

blocks.prompt: The Culture of Orcinus orca
blocks.text: Nothing about the orca is quite what it looks like. It is called a killer whale, but it is not a whale. It is a dolphin, the largest of them, and the name is a translation gone sideways. Spanish sailors called it asesina de ballenas, the killer of whales, and English took the words in the wrong order. Even the word species may not survive the next few decades of research. Consider the water off Washington State. Two kinds of orca share it. One group, the residents, eats fish and almost nothing else, mostly Chinook salmon. Another group, the Bigg's orcas, ignores fish completely and hunts seals, porpoises, and whale calves. The residents are talkative and travel in large families. The Bigg's orcas hunt in near silence, because seals can hear well and salmon largely cannot. The two use different calls, different group sizes, different methods. They pass each other in the same channel and do not interact. Genetic work suggests they have not interbred in hundreds of thousands of years. They look nearly identical. They are, biologically speaking, strangers. What separates them is not a mountain range or an ocean. It is culture. Orca hunting techniques are learned, and they are local. In Norway, pods herd herring into a tight ball and stun them with tail slaps. In Patagonia, pods deliberately beach themselves to take sea lion pups off the shore, a technique so dangerous that adults spend years coaching juveniles in shallow water first. In Antarctica, pods swim in formation to build a wave that washes seals off floating ice. In New Zealand, orcas hunt stingrays along the sea floor. Each of these is a tradition, invented once and taught ever since, and the pods that lack the tradition never think of it. Culture explains something else too. Female orcas stop having calves around the age of forty and then live for decades more, a pattern found in almost no other animal except humans. Long-term studies of the residents show why. When salmon are scarce, the oldest female leads the pod, and her grandcalves are far more likely to survive while she is alive. She carries the map of where food appears in a bad year. That knowledge takes eighty years to accumulate and one death to lose. Which brings the story somewhere uncomfortable. The Southern Residents, the most closely studied orcas on Earth, now number about seventy animals. Their salmon sit behind dams. Their water is crowded with engine noise, and an animal that hunts by sound in a loud ocean is hunting blind. Their bodies concentrate industrial chemicals released decades ago, and a mother passes much of her share to her first calf in her milk. Protecting orcas has usually been discussed as protecting animals. The residents suggest something harder. To save them you would have to save a body of knowledge, held in a few dozen aging heads, that no aquarium and no gene bank knows how to copy.
